scenario_extra.statement: The KEA uplift costs {{SPINE_COST_A}} and the PIT cut costs {{SPINE_COST_B}}. They are not the same size: about {{SPINE_GAP_PCT}} per cent apart, with {{SPINE_CHEAPER}} the cheaper of the two. Two reforms of different size cannot be compared on their absolute welfare effects, because the larger one moves more money and so scores higher at ε=0 whatever its targeting. The comparison here is therefore per euro of exchequer cost. On that measure the two are exactly equally efficient at ε=0, where the welfare measure is simply the money moved: 1.000 against 1.000. As ε rises the bottom-targeted transfer pulls ahead, reaching 1.572 against 0.862 at ε=1 and 2.512 against 0.846 at ε=2, because a euro reaching a poorer household counts for more while the tax cut's value falls away. The same pattern holds in all three EU tools. It is a statement about ratios, not about which reform is larger, and the per-euro columns of the table below are where to read it. (Why the −0.5pp cut and not the −1pp one on the menu: the −1pp cut costs about 1.9 times the KEA uplift, and on absolute welfare it is the higher of the two up to ε=1 purely because it is bigger. Per euro it is 0.859 against the uplift's 1.572 at ε=1, so the size of the tax cut chosen does not change the per-euro answer.)

It is distributionally weighted euros, not simply the total euros gained. Shown in 2024 euros (×1.0321).

unemployment_caveat: The exchequer cost of the unemployment scenarios EXCLUDES the contributory unemployment-benefit response and therefore UNDERSTATES the true fiscal cost: the model's les-flip mechanism removes earnings but does not confer unemployment-benefit eligibility.
capacity_caveat: The capacity and shock model is INDICATIVE: it uses UK-derived operational parameters (demand elasticities and staff ratios), scaled to this country's own {{UNITS}} but not Greece-calibrated. The shock magnitudes are computed points on this country's own surface, but the share of {{UNITS}} losing an earner is the UK's own share, applied to this country's own WORKING-AGE unit count so that the base matches the one the UK measures the share on. Treat the demand, utilisation and gap figures as order-of-magnitude, not a local forecast.
provenance: EU-SILC 2024 wave; income reference year 2023; EUROMOD policy system 2023 (EL_2023). Analyst welfare, distributional and fiscal results come from the validated response surface (the fiscal figures are its re-emitted net exchequer cost). Analyst monetary values are 2023 nominal EUR shown in 2024 EUR (×1.0321, Eurostat nama_10_gdp B1GQ PD15_NAC); Provider values are 2024-equivalent EUR. GDP and unemployment figures inherit Greece's self-employment under-capture (~0.48x). Built on the EU-SILC data, run through EUROMOD rather than EUROMOD's own bundled input dataset (the EMSD), which applies EUROMOD's own harmonisation and imputation; welfare and distributional results are validated against the EUROMOD Country-Report baseline, and the effect on fiscal levels of running EU-SILC directly rather than the EMSD is unquantified (neither equivalent to a standard EUROMOD run nor inferior, only prepared differently). The conversion populates 55 input columns, including the property tax the model reads. What is still missing is the national-SILC benefit components, the pension-fund and hazardous-work variables, the main-residence floor area, and the NUTS-2 region, for which the release carries NUTS-1 only. Aggregates only; no microdata.
home_html:
About the project

BENEFITS develops a Holistic Appraisal Framework (HAF) to measure the social, economic and environmental value-added of social services. HAF combines real household microdata and tax-benefit microsimulation with “beyond GDP” valuation methods to quantify how policy reforms and social services affect people's welfare. Findings are consolidated through a Social Services Policy Observatory and citizen assemblies, supported by a Visualisations Platform, and built into a Policy Evaluation Toolkit to inform policymaking.

Full title: Building Economic, Needs-Based and Environmental evaluation Frameworks for Inclusive Transformation of Social services in Europe. Coordinator: KMOP, with 10 partners across 7 countries. Funding: Horizon Europe, grant agreement no. 101179032.

About this tool

This is the Greek edition of the Microsimulation Valuation Tool. It lets you move each reform family continuously across its modelled range and read the distributional welfare, fiscal, and provider responses for Greece. It reads a pre-computed response surface ({{POINTS_PER_DIAL}}, each already passed through the welfare layer, computed on EUROMOD EL_2023 over the EU-SILC 2024 wave) and interpolates linearly between those points as you drag a slider. It does not run the tax-benefit engine live using microdata, and ships only aggregate welfare, distributional and fiscal results, no microdata. All monetary values are in 2024 euros: 2023 nominal values uprated by the Greek GDP deflator, ×1.0321.

⚠ Greek income-side caveat. Greece's self-employment income is captured at about 0.48x national accounts. The earnings-downturn (GDP) and unemployment dials and scenarios inherit this, so their income-side effects and fiscal costs are understated - read those figures as lower bounds.

The {{DIAL_COUNT}} dials

  • Minimum income (KEA, Social Solidarity Income): increases the payment to existing recipients by 0 to +50%. KEA sets its guaranteed amount separately for adults and for children.
  • Child benefit A21: increases the allowance by 0 to +50%. Tier amounts are about €70 and €140 a month per child.
  • Personal Income Tax (PIT) first-bracket rate: changes the 9% rate on income up to €10,000 across the modelled range, from a 5 percentage point (pp) cut to a 5pp rise. This is a rate change, not a change to the tax-free allowance.
  • Earnings downturn (market income): reduces market income by 0 to 10%, a direct earnings cut, not job losses.
  • Unemployment shock: raises unemployment by 0 to 10pp, modelled as that share of employed people losing their earnings.

One reform at a time

The tool enforces single-reform exploration: exactly one control is active at any moment, and moving any control resets the others to baseline. The response surface is calculated one reform at a time; combining two reforms is not the sum of their separate effects, because reforms interact, so the tool will not show a number it cannot stand behind.

Inequality aversion (ε)

ε sets how much more a €1 welfare gain to a lower-income household counts than the same €1 to a higher-income household. It is a value judgement you choose, not a result the tool dictates; as you change ε, the welfare figure updates to reflect it.

  • ε = 0: every €1 counts equally, regardless of income (pure efficiency; the utilitarian case).
  • ε = 1: the standard central value, a €1 gain to a household at or below the at-risk-of-poverty line counts about 1.7 times as much as the same €1 to a household on the median.
  • ε = 2: strong inequality aversion, the same gain counts about 2.8 times. That is the maximum: the living standard is floored at the at-risk-of-poverty line (AROP), 60% of the median, before the weight is taken.

A bottom-targeted reform, such as a higher minimum income guarantee, grows more valuable as ε rises; a reform whose gains sit higher up the distribution, such as a tax rate cut, shrinks as ε rises.

How to use it

Analyst mode. Set ε, then move one dial and read the results: the welfare effect, the ε strip (how that effect changes across ε values), the fiscal cost, the winners-and-losers split, and the decile chart. The other controls snap back to baseline whenever you move one.

Provider mode. Enter a caseload and targeting profile, then read the value ladder (defined below). Every value shown includes its source and provenance. The capacity-gap and shock views are indicative only. Their demand elasticities and staff ratios are registry assumptions rather than measured national figures, and the share of {{UNITS}} losing an earner is the UK's own share applied to this country's WORKING-AGE unit count, matching the base the UK measures that share on, so only that base is local.

The value ladder, a stepped set of value estimates, from the most conservative at the bottom to the fullest at the top:

  • Cash floor: the value counting only the direct cash the service moves (benefits paid or income secured). A deliberately conservative lower bound.
  • Headline: the cash floor plus the monetised value of the service's wider social outcomes, for example wellbeing gains. The main figure to quote.
  • Low/central/high band: the range around the headline, reflecting genuine uncertainty in those social-outcome values.

Scenarios mode. {{SCENARIO_COUNT_CAP}} fixed reforms and shocks, each with its fiscal cost, distributional effect, welfare, and cost-effectiveness, plus the spine, which compares the minimum income uplift with the tax cut per euro of exchequer cost rather than on their absolute effects, because the two reforms are not the same size. Per euro they are exactly equally efficient at ε = 0, where the welfare measure is just the money moved, and the uplift pulls ahead as ε rises.

Data year: EU-SILC 2024 wave; income reference year 2023; EUROMOD policy system EL_2023. Built on the EU-SILC data (2024 wave), run through EUROMOD - not EUROMOD's own bundled input dataset (the EMSD), which prepares its inputs with EUROMOD's own harmonisation and imputation. The welfare and distributional results are validated against the EUROMOD Country-Report baseline; the effect of this input difference on the fiscal figures is not quantified. Aggregates only; no microdata.

gdp_shock.label: Earnings downturn (market income)
gdp_shock.base: Market income (employees' and self-employed earnings, yem/yse, plus yemre/ysere for Greece) is scaled down by the shown percentage; baseline is 0%. This is an across-the-board earnings cut for people in work, not job losses. NOTE: Greece's self-employment income is captured at only about 0.48x national accounts, so the income-side effect of this shock - and the lost tax and social contributions it implies - is UNDERSTATED here; read the fiscal figure as a lower bound.
gdp_shock.explain: An earnings downturn lowers households' incomes and the tax and contributions they pay, which is why it costs the exchequer (lost revenue).
gdp_shock.winlose: Working households across the distribution lose a little earnings; the near-zero winners share is low-income households whose means-tested support rises slightly as earnings fall.

pit_give.label: PIT first-bracket rate change
pit_give.base: Greece's personal income tax first-bracket rate is 9% (on income up to €10,000; the tin00_rate1 constant). Baseline is 0 pp. The dial cuts this rate by the shown percentage points. A tax-free-allowance dial is not offered because no single such constant is exposed in the model, so the lever is a rate cut.
pit_give.explain: Cutting the PIT first-bracket rate returns money to income-tax payers, who sit in the middle and upper parts of the distribution, so its welfare value falls as the weight on poorer households (ε) rises.
pit_give.winlose: Winners are income-tax payers in the middle and upper-middle deciles; the poorest gain little because they pay little income tax. There are no losers.

child_benefit_up.label: Child benefit A21
child_benefit_up.base: Greece's A21 child benefit (the bch instrument), with tier amounts of about €70 and €140 per month per child. Baseline is 0%; the dial raises the A21 amounts by the shown percentage.
child_benefit_up.explain: Raising A21 helps families with children; because A21 is targeted lower down the distribution, the gain is concentrated in lower and middle deciles and its welfare value holds up as ε rises.
child_benefit_up.winlose: Winners are families with children, concentrated lower down the distribution; there are no losers.

min_income_up.label: KEA minimum income: higher payment to existing recipients
min_income_up.base: Greece's KEA guaranteed minimum income, the EUROMOD bsa00 instrument, whose guaranteed amount is set separately per adult and per child ($bsa00_adult_amt and $bsa00_child_amt). Baseline is 0%. The dial raises the guaranteed payment to households already receiving KEA by the shown percentage; it holds eligibility fixed and does not model new recipients or take-up expansion (an income-floor top-up, like Spain's IMV).
min_income_up.explain: A higher KEA payment is a pure transfer to the poorest households (there are no losers), so its welfare value grows as the weight on poorer households (ε) rises. KEA is small, so the euro effect is modest.
min_income_up.winlose: Winners are the poorest households already on KEA; there are no losers, because the uplift is funded from general taxation rather than from other claimants.

unemployment_shock.label: Unemployment shock
unemployment_shock.base: Baseline is 0 pp. The dial raises unemployment by the shown percentage points, modelled as that share of employed people losing their earnings (a nested les-flip for monotonicity). NOTE: Greece's self-employment income is captured at only about 0.48x national accounts, so the income-side effect of this shock - and the lost tax and social contributions it implies - is UNDERSTATED here; read the fiscal figure as a lower bound.
unemployment_shock.explain: A rise in unemployment removes earnings from the people who lose their jobs. The modelled fiscal cost excludes the contributory unemployment-benefit response and therefore understates the true cost.
unemployment_shock.winlose: Losers are the households pushed out of work; the small winners share is households the benefit system more than compensates for a modest earnings loss. The exchequer cost shown excludes the contributory unemployment-benefit response.

profiles_provenance_note: Targeting bands defined as decile groups (1 to 3, 4 to 6, and all ten). A presentational choice about which part of the distribution a service serves, with no source; the user selects among them.

scenarios.label: Higher KEA payment +10%
scenarios.desc: The KEA minimum-income guarantee for existing recipients rises 10% (no take-up expansion).
scenarios.winlose: Winners are the low-income households already receiving KEA; near-zero losers because the uplift is funded from general taxation, not from other claimants.

scenarios.label: Higher KEA payment +25%
scenarios.desc: The KEA guarantee for existing recipients rises 25%.
scenarios.winlose: Winners are existing KEA recipients in the lowest deciles; near-zero losers (funded from general taxation).

scenarios.label: Higher KEA payment +50%
scenarios.desc: The KEA guarantee for existing recipients rises 50%. Spine scenario.
scenarios.winlose: Winners are the poorest households on KEA; there are no losers because the uplift is funded from general taxation.

scenarios.label: PIT first-bracket -0.5pp
scenarios.desc: The PIT first-bracket rate (9%) is cut by 0.5pp. Spine scenario (the tax cut whose exchequer cost matches the KEA +50% uplift).
scenarios.winlose: Winners are income-tax payers in the middle and upper-middle deciles; the poorest gain little because they pay little income tax. No losers.

scenarios.label: PIT first-bracket -1pp
scenarios.desc: The PIT first-bracket rate (9%) is cut by 1pp.
scenarios.winlose: Winners are income-tax payers up the distribution; the very bottom gains little. No losers.

scenarios.label: PIT first-bracket -2pp
scenarios.desc: The PIT first-bracket rate is cut by 2pp.
scenarios.winlose: Winners are income-tax payers in the middle and upper deciles. No losers.

scenarios.label: PIT first-bracket -5pp
scenarios.desc: The PIT first-bracket rate is cut by 5pp.
scenarios.winlose: A broad income-tax cut; gains concentrated in middle and upper deciles. No losers.

scenarios.label: Child benefit A21 +10%
scenarios.winlose: Winners are families with children, concentrated lower down the distribution; no losers.

services.name: Employment support
services.flag: Closest available estimate: 0.46 WELLBY at the €13,317 spine (HM Treasury Wellbeing Guidance 2021: £13,000 at 2019 prices, uprated and PPP-adjusted to Greece); transferred from the UK Britain fixed-effects unemployment-to-employment coefficient as no Greek figure exists. That gives €6,126 for one person moving into work, within a €4,713 to €7,540 band. THAT IS NOT THE VALUE THIS TOOL APPLIES: it is the wellbeing figure before the two valuation stages. The tool applies €404 per person re-employed, within a €104 to €937 band, being that figure times an effect share of 0.30 (0.11 low, 0.46 high) and an attribution of 0.22 (0.20 low, 0.27 high). Both quantities are per person re-employed, which is why the smaller one is named here: quoting €6,126 as the value overstates it about fifteenfold. The stages, their sources and every denominator are on the value's own note.

NOT ADOPTED. Greece holds a national figure of its own, methadone at EUR 1.8 per day medication-only at about 2009-10, EUR 657 a year native and EUR 2.07 per day or EUR 754 a year once uprated by 1.147861. It is not adopted because it is a different quantity from the one this row holds. This row is a per-case cost of DELIVERING opioid substitution, and the Spanish figure it converts from is explicitly EXCLUDING MEDICATION. The Greek figure is the medication alone, which the evidence record flags at roughly a third of full delivery cost. The two are complements and not alternatives, so adopting the Greek one would put a drug price in a delivery-cost row and would leave the Greek cell measuring something neither the Spanish nor the Italian cell measures, which is the comparability the three-country set exists to hold. THE NON-ADOPTION IS NOT NEUTRAL, and the direction is worth stating: EUR 754 for the medication alone against EUR 865 shipped for the whole delivery is not credible, and this cell is more likely too low than too high, and by a factor rather than a margin. The shipped EUR 865 is a labour-cost conversion of a Spanish delivery cost that EXCLUDES MEDICATION; the only Greek national datum is medication ALONE, EUR 754 once uprated, which is 87 per cent of it. A component the evidence record flags at roughly a third of full delivery cannot credibly be 87 per cent of that delivery, and grossing the national figure to full scope on that same one-third flag gives about EUR 2,262, some 2.6 times the shipped value. IT IS DECLARED RATHER THAN CORRECTED because the one-third is a qualitative note in the evidence record and not a measured ratio, so raising the cell on it would put an invented number on the face; and because this row is COST-INPUT with a value-added of zero, so the understatement reaches the extra-running-cost line and no value. Correcting it needs a Greek delivery-cost source that includes staff time, which three stages of searching did not find.

Employment support.provenance_note: 0.46 WELLBY transferred from the UK Britain fixed-effects coefficient (Clark et al. 2018), valued on this country's PPP-adjusted spine, then staged. Transfer with a stated adjustment. ORIGIN 16300 FACTOR 0.37581816; BAND ORIGIN 12540 AND 20064; STAGE EFFECT 0.11 0.30 0.46 ATTRIBUTION 0.20 0.22 0.27. The origin is the UK WELLBY spine at 2024 prices and its low and high tiers; the factor is the household-final-consumption PPP to Greece, 0.816996, times the 0.46 coefficient. The stages apply in all four tools. An attribution share is the tool's convention rather than a national fact, so it needs no national warrant; the effect share is an empirical value borrowed between countries and is flagged as such below. EFFECT SHARE, an OUTCOME RATE, and a BORROWED one: 0.30 central from the Work and Health Programme job-outcome rate of 31 per cent and the Restart Scheme rate of 30 per cent, 0.11 low from Additional Work Coach Support, 0.46 high from the Work and Health Programme first-earnings rate. These are BRITISH PROGRAMME RATES APPLIED WITHOUT NATIONAL ADJUSTMENT, on a denominator of programme starts. No equivalent national rate exists for this country, and the national active labour market policy evidence is carried as a qualitative warrant only, with no effect size, by the project's own standing rule. ATTRIBUTION, an IMPACT: 0.22 central within a sourced range of 0.20, the Department for Work and Pensions' own Restart additionality projection of six in a hundred over the thirty in a hundred reaching a job outcome THE SIX IN A HUNDRED IS THE DEPARTMENT'S OWN BUSINESS-CASE PROJECTION AND NOT A STATISTICAL FINDING. It is published in House of Commons Committee of Public Accounts, The Restart Scheme for Long-term Unemployed People, Forty-Second Report of Session 2022-23, HC 733, 22 March 2023, at Conclusions and recommendations paragraph 1, where the committee quotes the Department's expectation of a return of 2.44 pounds for every pound spent and its estimate that an extra six in a hundred participants will find sustained work above what would have happened anyway, and warns in the same sentence that if that estimate is too high the benefits of the scheme will quickly fall away. The committee measured nothing here; it is reporting what the Department expected., and 0.27, the three-percentage-point Additional Work Coach Support impact over its eleven per cent in-work rate. THE PUBLICATION IS Department for Work and Pensions, The impact of additional Jobcentre Plus support on the employment outcomes of disabled people, research and analysis, 18 March 2025, which states that twelve months after the intervention 11 per cent of participants were in work compared to 8 per cent of the comparison group, a 3 percentage point employment impact, and that the impact is statistically significant. It is NOT the qualitative report The experience of Additional Work Coach Support of 2 May 2025, which carries no percentage at all and refers the reader to this impact analysis. A LATER PUBLICATION RESTATES THE SAME TWELVE-MONTH COMPARISON AND THIS VALUE DOES NOT FOLLOW IT: the extended impact assessment at 24 months, Official Statistics, 25 March 2026, gives 11 per cent against 8.2 per cent, an impact of 2.8 percentage points, which on the same arithmetic would put this bound at 2.8 over 11 = 0.2545 rather than 0.2727. The shipped 0.27 is the March 2025 figure and is unchanged; the restatement is recorded here so the difference is accounted for rather than left for a reader to find. meta.poverty_basis: Two thresholds, both emitted at every point. RELATIVE (relative_*): 60% of that point's own weighted median equivalised (OECD-modified) household disposable income, the published AROP convention and the same line the social weight uses as its floor; it moves with the reform, so a reform that lowers the median lowers the line and can cut the measured count without raising anyone's income. ANCHORED (anchored_*): the same 60%-of-median line computed once at the zero-magnitude baseline point and held fixed across every point of every dial, emitted as anchored_bhc_threshold_cur so it is auditable; internally defined, needing no external source, and the right comparison of a reform against its own baseline. ANCHORED IS NOT ABSOLUTE: the absolute_* fields mean a fixed EXTERNAL base year and stay null because no sourced one exists for ES, IT or EL. The AHC fields are null throughout because the EUROMOD per-unit layer carries no housing-cost concept. All other field names follow the UK surface exactly.
meta.rebuild: Built on EUROMOD v3.8.6, on a COMPLETED input conversion. Every input variable a live 2023 policy reads, for which the EUROMOD input data codebook publishes a recipe and whose sources the public EU-SILC user database carries, is populated from that recipe: Spain carries 68 populated input columns, Greece 55, Italy 44. The consequential ones are Spain's pension and unemployment decompositions and its rent, mortgage and private-pension deductions; Greece's property tax, which is the ENFIA the model reads and passes through; and Italy's contract class, without which no employer contribution fires at all. A surface is a function of its inputs, so reproducing a stored surface is not the test; the test is agreement with each country's own published EUROMOD baseline, recorded in europe/docs/BASELINE_VALIDATION.md. Conventions this surface holds: the stable sort in build_grid.point_from_pu and in wevm._weighted_median / wevm.wevm_by_decile, the two-sided pit_give grid, and the fiscal and poverty objects emitted in the same pass, fiscal by the method of re_emit.py. Poverty carries both a relative (moving) and an anchored (held at baseline) threshold; see poverty_basis.

min_income_up.detail: This dial's means test has an asset leg that cannot be applied: the KEA reads the floor area of the household's main residence, and the public EU-SILC user database this build converts does not carry it, so no household is excluded on property. The direction of the error is established, and it runs downwards rather than upwards. Three figures, all of them cells of the same row of the same table (Greece country report Y16_CR_EL, table A3.6): the scheme is published as spending EUR 520m in 2023, sourced to the Greek General Accounting Office; this build models EUR 495.7m, 4.7 per cent below it; and EUROMOD's own simulation is EUR 426m, 18.1 per cent below it. Same scheme, same year, same table, so the comparison is like for like. The published figure is not merely a comparator, it is the target the model aims at: Greece runs EUROMOD's Benefit Calibration Adjustment with EUR 520m as its expenditure target, and because the modelled outlay never reaches that target the cap never binds and every eligible household is paid. An asset test only removes eligible units, so applying the missing leg would take this dial further below the published spend rather than closer to it. On the measured range of 8.9 to 16.7 per cent of outlay it would land between EUR 413m and EUR 452m, which brackets EUROMOD's own EUR 426m and is further from EUR 520m than this build is. The financial capital leg was implemented from the codebook recipe, measured, and not shipped, because the investment income it capitalises is captured at 0.05 of the external figure in the same report. The adjustment's switch state and its target are read from the model by europe/model/benefit_adjustments.py.
